#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""

        self.o = cls(10)


def test_exact_issue_scenario():
    """Test the exact scenario from the GitHub issue."""
    print("Testing exact scenario from GitHub issue...")
    
    parser = ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_class_arguments(B, 'B')

    except Exception as e:

        return False


def test_consistency_between_type_and_Type():
    """Test that builtins.type and typing.Type behave consistently."""
    print("\nTesting consistency between builtins.type and typing.Type...")
    
    from typing import Type
    
    # Test with typing.Type (was working before)
    class B_Type:
        def __init__(self, cls: Type = A):
            self.o = cls(10)

    class B_builtin_type:
        def __init__(self, cls: type = A):
            self.o = cls(10)
            
    # Test with parametrized builtins.type (was working before)
    class B_parametrized_type:
        def __init__(self, cls: type[A] = A):
            self.o = cls(10)
    
    results = []
    
    # Test typing.Type
    try:
        parser = ArgumentParser()
        parser.add_class_arguments(B_Type, 'B_Type')

    92	### C++ Custom Op Compatibility
    93	TensorFlow C++ APIs are not stable and thus we can only guarantee compatibility with the 
    94	version TensorFlow Addons was built against. It is possible custom ops will work with multiple 
    95	versions of TensorFlow, but there is also a chance for segmentation faults or other problematic crashes.
    96	Warnings will be emitted when loading a custom op if your TensorFlow version does not match 
    97	what it was built against.
    98	
    99	Additionally, custom ops registration does not have a stable ABI interface so it is 
   100	required that users have a compatible installation of TensorFlow even if the versions 
   101	match what we had built against. A simplification of this is that **TensorFlow Addons 
   102	custom ops will work with `pip`-installed TensorFlow** but will have issues when TensorFlow 
   103	is compiled differently. A typical example of this would be `conda`-installed TensorFlow.
   104	[RFC #133](https://github.com/tensorflow/community/pull/133) aims to fix this.

   176	## Core Concepts
   177	
   178	#### Standardized API within Subpackages
   179	User experience and project maintainability are core concepts in
   180	TensorFlow Addons. In order to achieve these we require that our additions
   181	conform to established API patterns seen in core TensorFlow.
   182	
   183	#### GPU and CPU Custom Ops
   184	TensorFlow Addons supports precompiled custom ops for CPU and GPU. However, 
   185	GPU custom ops currently only work on Linux distributions. For this reason Windows and macOS 
   186	will fallback to pure TensorFlow Python implementations whenever possible.
   187	
   188	The order of priority on macOS/Windows is:
   189	1) Pure TensorFlow + Python implementation (works on CPU and GPU)
   190	2) C++ implementation for CPU
   191	
   192	The order of priority on Linux is:
   193	1) CUDA implementation
   194	2) C++ implementation
   195	3) Pure TensorFlow + Python implementation (works on CPU and GPU)
   196	
   197	If you want to change the default priority, "C++ and CUDA" VS "pure TensorFlow Python",
   198	you can set the environment variable `TF_ADDONS_PY_OPS=1` from the command line or
   199	run `tfa.options.disable_custom_kernel()` in your code.
   200	
   201	For example, if you are on Linux and you have compatibility problems with the compiled ops,
   202	you can give priority to the Python implementations:
   203	
   204	From the command line:
   205	```bash
   206	export TF_ADDONS_PY_OPS=1
   207	```
   208	
   209	or in your code:
   210	
   211	```python
   212	import tensorflow_addons as tfa
   213	tfa.options.disable_custom_kernel()
   214	```
   215	
   216	This variable defaults to `True` on Windows and macOS, and `False` on Linux.
   217	
   218	#### Proxy Maintainership
   219	TensorFlow Addons has been designed to compartmentalize submodules so 
   220	that they can be maintained by community users who have expertise, and a vested 
   221	interest in that component. We heavily encourage users to submit sign up to maintain a 
   222	submodule by submitting your username to the [CODEOWNERS](.github/CODEOWNERS) file.
   223	
   224	Full write access will only be granted after substantial contribution 
   225	has been made in order to limit the number of users with write permission. 
   226	Contributions can come in the form of issue closings, bug fixes, documentation, 
   227	new code, or optimizing existing code. Submodule maintainership can be granted 
   228	with a lower barrier for entry as this will not include write permissions to 
   229	the repo.
   230	
   231	For more information see [the RFC](https://github.com/tensorflow/community/blob/master/rfcs/20190308-addons-proxy-maintainership.md) 
   232	on this topic.
   233	
   234	#### Periodic Evaluation of Subpackages
   235	Given the nature of this repository, submodules may become less 
   236	and less useful to the community as time goes on. In order to keep the 
   237	repository sustainable, we'll be performing bi-annual reviews of our code to 
   238	ensure everything still belongs within the repo. Contributing factors to this 
   239	review will be:
   240	
   241	1. Number of active maintainers
   242	2. Amount of OSS use
   243	3. Amount of issues or bugs attributed to the code
   244	4. If a better solution is now available
   245	
   246	Functionality within TensorFlow Addons can be categorized into three groups:
   247	
   248	* **Suggested**: well-maintained API; use is encouraged.
   249	* **Discouraged**: a better alternative is available; the API is kept for 
   250	historic reasons; or the API requires maintenance and is the waiting period 
   251	to be deprecated.
   252	* **Deprecated**: use at your own risk; subject to be deleted.
   253	
   254	The status change between these three groups is: 
   255	Suggested <-> Discouraged -> Deprecated.
   256	
   257	The period between an API being marked as deprecated and being deleted will be 
   258	90 days. The rationale being:
   259	
   260	1. In the event that TensorFlow Addons releases monthly, there will be 2-3 
   261	releases before an API is deleted. The release notes could give user enough 
   262	warning.
   263	
   264	2. 90 days gives maintainers ample time to fix their code.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Reproduction script for NovoGrad float64 issue.
This script reproduces the exact issue described in the bug report.
"""

import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow_addons.optimizers import NovoGrad


def test_fit_simple_linear_model():
    np.random.seed(0x2020)
    tf.random.set_seed(0x2020)

    x = np.random.standard_normal((100000, 3))
    w = np.random.standard_normal((3, 1))
    y = np.dot(x, w) + np.random.standard_normal((100000, 1)) * 1e-5

    model = tf.keras.models.Sequential()
    model.add(tf.keras.layers.Dense(input_shape=(3,), units=1))
    model.compile(NovoGrad(), loss="mse")

    model.fit(x, y, epochs=2)

    x = np.random.standard_normal((100, 3))
    y = np.dot(x, w)
    predicted = model.predict(x)

    max_abs_diff = np.max(np.abs(predicted - y))
    assert max_abs_diff < 1e-2
    print(f"Max absolute difference: {max_abs_diff}")
    

if __name__ == "__main__":

        print("SUCCESS: float64 backend works!")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Comprehensive test for NovoGrad float64 support.
Tests various scenarios to ensure robustness.
"""

import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow_addons.optimizers import NovoGrad


def test_basic_functionality():
    """Test basic functionality with both float32 and float64."""
    print("Testing basic functionality...")
    
    # Test data
    x = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype=np.float32)
    y = np.array([[0.0], [1.0]], dtype=np.float32)
    
    for dtype_name, dtype_val in [('float32', 'float32'), ('float64', 'float64')]:
        print(f"  Testing with {dtype_name} backend...")
        tf.keras.backend.set_floatx(dtype_val)
        
        # Create model
        model = tf.keras.Sequential([
            tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, input_shape=(2,))
        ])
        model.compile(optimizer=NovoGrad(learning_rate=0.01), loss='mse')
        
        # Train briefly
        model.fit(x, y, epochs=2, verbose=0)
        
        # Make prediction
        pred = model.predict(x[:1], verbose=0)
        assert pred.shape == (1, 1), f"Prediction shape incorrect for {dtype_name}"
        
    print("  Basic functionality test passed!")


def test_with_weight_decay():
    """Test with weight decay enabled."""
    print("Testing with weight decay...")
    
    x = np.random.randn(100, 5).astype(np.float32)
    y = np.sum(x[:, :2], axis=1, keepdims=True)
    
    for dtype_name, dtype_val in [('float32', 'float32'), ('float64', 'float64')]:
        print(f"  Testing with {dtype_name} backend and weight decay...")
        tf.keras.backend.set_floatx(dtype_val)
        
        model = tf.keras.Sequential([
            tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='relu', input_shape=(5,)),
            tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)
        ])
        model.compile(optimizer=NovoGrad(learning_rate=0.01, weight_decay=0.01), loss='mse')
        
        # Brief training
        history = model.fit(x, y, epochs=3, verbose=0)
        assert len(history.history['loss']) == 3, f"Training failed for {dtype_name}"
        
    print("  Weight decay test passed!")


def test_sparse_gradients():
    """Test with sparse gradients (embedding lookup)."""
    print("Testing with sparse gradients...")
    
    # Simple embedding task
    vocab_size = 100
    embed_dim = 10
    seq_length = 5
    
    # Sample data
    x = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (50, seq_length))
    y = np.random.randn(50, 1)
    
    for dtype_name, dtype_val in [('float32', 'float32'), ('float64', 'float64')]:
        print(f"  Testing sparse gradients with {dtype_name} backend...")
        tf.keras.backend.set_floatx(dtype_val)
        
        model = tf.keras.Sequential([
            tf.keras.layers.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, input_length=seq_length),
            tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D(),
            tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)
        ])
        model.compile(optimizer=NovoGrad(learning_rate=0.01), loss='mse')
        
        # Brief training
        history = model.fit(x, y, epochs=2, verbose=0)
        assert len(history.history['loss']) == 2, f"Sparse gradient training failed for {dtype_name}"
        
    print("  Sparse gradients test passed!")


def test_different_novograd_configs():
    """Test different NovoGrad configurations."""
    print("Testing different NovoGrad configurations...")
    
    x = np.random.randn(50, 3).astype(np.float32)
    y = np.sum(x[:, :2], axis=1, keepdims=True)
    
    configs = [
        {"grad_averaging": True},
        {"grad_averaging": False}, 
        {"weight_decay": 0.01, "grad_averaging": True},
        {"weight_decay": 0.001, "grad_averaging": False},
        {"amsgrad": True}
    ]
    
    for i, config in enumerate(configs):
        for dtype_name, dtype_val in [('float32', 'float32'), ('float64', 'float64')]:
            print(f"  Testing config {i+1} with {dtype_name} backend...")
            tf.keras.backend.set_floatx(dtype_val)
            
            model = tf.keras.Sequential([
                tf.keras.layers.Dense(5, activation='relu', input_shape=(3,)),
                tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)
            ])
            optimizer = NovoGrad(learning_rate=0.01, **config)
            model.compile(optimizer=optimizer, loss='mse')
            
            # Brief training
            history = model.fit(x, y, epochs=2, verbose=0)
            assert len(history.history['loss']) == 2, f"Config {i+1} failed for {dtype_name}"
            
    print("  Different configurations test passed!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Running comprehensive NovoGrad tests...\n")
    
    try:
        test_basic_functionality()
        print()
        test_with_weight_decay()
        print()
        test_sparse_gradients()
        print()
        test_different_novograd_configs()
        print()
        print("All tests passed! 🎉")
        
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"\n❌ Test failed with error: {e}")
        raise

"""
Exact reproduction of the issue described in the bug report.
This is the exact code from the issue that was failing.
"""

import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow_addons.optimizers import NovoGrad


def test_fit_simple_linear_model():
    np.random.seed(0x2020)
    tf.random.set_seed(0x2020)

    x = np.random.standard_normal((100000, 3))
    w = np.random.standard_normal((3, 1))
    y = np.dot(x, w) + np.random.standard_normal((100000, 1)) * 1e-5

    model = tf.keras.models.Sequential()
    model.add(tf.keras.layers.Dense(input_shape=(3,), units=1))
    model.compile(NovoGrad(), loss="mse")

    model.fit(x, y, epochs=2)

    x = np.random.standard_normal((100, 3))
    y = np.dot(x, w)
    predicted = model.predict(x)

    max_abs_diff = np.max(np.abs(predicted - y))
    assert max_abs_diff < 1e-2
    

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Running exact reproduction from bug report...")
    
    # Test with float32 (this was always working)
    print("Testing with float32 backend...")
    tf.keras.backend.set_floatx('float32')
    test_fit_simple_linear_model()
    print("✅ float32 test passed")
    
    # Test with float64 (this was failing before our fix)
    print("Testing with float64 backend...")
    tf.keras.backend.set_floatx('float64')
    test_fit_simple_linear_model()
    print("✅ float64 test passed")
    
    print("\n🎉 Issue has been resolved! Both float32 and float64 backends work correctly.")

     2	
     3	Shrink Ray is a modern multiformat test-case reducer.
     4	
     5	It's designed to be highly parallel, and work with a very wide variety of formats, through a mix of good generic algorithms and format-specific reduction passes.

    57	
    58	Shrink Ray is fully generic in the sense that it will work with literally any file you give it in any format. However, some formats will work a lot better than others.
    59	
    60	It has a generic reduction algorithm that should work pretty well with any textual format, and an architecture that is designed to make it easy to add specialised support for specific formats as needed.

    30	Pint: makes units easy
    31	======================
    32	
    33	Pint is a Python package to define, operate and manipulate physical
    34	quantities: the product of a numerical value and a unit of measurement.
    35	It allows arithmetic operations between them and conversions from and
    36	to different units.
    37	
    38	It is distributed with a comprehensive list of physical units, prefixes
    39	and constants. Due to its modular design, you can extend (or even rewrite!)
    40	the complete list without changing the source code. It supports a lot of
    41	numpy mathematical operations **without monkey patching or wrapping numpy**.
    42	
    43	It has a complete test coverage. It runs in Python 3.6+ with no other dependency.
    44	If you need Python 2.7 or 3.4/3.5 compatibility, use Pint 0.9.
    45	It is licensed under BSD.
    46	
    47	It is extremely easy and natural to use:

    50	
    51	    >>> import pint
    52	    >>> ureg = pint.UnitRegistry()
    53	    >>> 3 * ureg.meter + 4 * ureg.cm

   106

   108	quantities, no one was really fitting my needs. Like most developers, I
   109	programmed Pint to scratch my own itches.
   110	
   111	**Unit parsing**: prefixed and pluralized forms of units are recognized without
   112	explicitly defining them. In other words: as the prefix *kilo* and the unit
   113	*meter* are defined, Pint understands *kilometers*. This results in a much
   114	shorter and maintainable unit definition list as compared to other packages.
   115	
   116	**Standalone unit definitions**: units definitions are loaded from a text file
   117	which is simple and easy to edit. Adding and changing units and their
   118	definitions does not involve changing the code.
   119	
   120	**Advanced string formatting**: a quantity can be formatted into string using
   121	`PEP 3101`_ syntax. Extended conversion flags are given to provide symbolic,
   122	LaTeX and pretty formatting. Unit name translation is available if Babel_ is
   123	installed.
   124	
   125	**Free to choose the numerical type**: You can use any numerical type
   126	(`fraction`, `float`, `decimal`, `numpy.ndarray`, etc). NumPy_ is not required

Let me clearly state the problem and solution:

**Problem:** 
When multiple contexts redefine the same unit, pint incorrectly uses the FIRST redefinition instead of the LATEST one. This happens because in `_switch_context_cache_and_units()`, redefinitions are applied in the order they appear in `self._active_ctx.contexts`, but this list has the latest context LAST, so it gets overridden by earlier contexts.

**Location:** 
The problem is in `/workspace/hgrecco__pint__0.12/pint/registry.py` at line 1549 in the `_switch_context_cache_and_units()` method.

**How the test reproduces the issue:**
1. Create context c1: lb = 0.5 kg
2. Create context c2: lb = 0.7 kg  
3. Enable c1 → 1 kg = 2 lb ✓
4. Enable c2 → Should be 1 kg = 1.428... lb, but stays 2 lb ❌

**Best practices for the fix:**
- Make minimal change
- Follow the same pattern as transformations (which work correctly)
- Don't break existing functionality
- The fix should align with the documented behavior that "last context takes precedence"

**How to fix:**
Change line 1549 from:
`for ctx in self._active_ctx.contexts:`
to:
`for ctx in reversed(self._active_ctx.contexts):`

This ensures that the LATEST context's redefinitions are applied LAST, thus overriding earlier ones, which matches the expected behavior and how transformations work.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Test specifically for the GitHub issue fix:
"Context redefinitions can't be overlayed"

This test verifies that when multiple contexts are active and more than one 
redefines the same unit, pint correctly picks up the latest redefinition 
instead of the first one.
"""

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, '/workspace/hgrecco__pint__0.12')

import pint


def test_context_redefinition_overlay_fix():
    """Test that context redefinitions properly overlay - latest wins."""
    
    # Create registry and contexts as in the issue
    ureg = pint.UnitRegistry()
    c1 = pint.Context.from_lines(["@context a", "lb = 0.5 kg"])
    c2 = pint.Context.from_lines(["@context b", "lb = 0.7 kg"])
    one_kg = ureg.Quantity(1, "kg")
    
    # Default conversion
    default_lb = one_kg.to("lb")
    assert abs(default_lb.magnitude - 2.2046226218487757) < 1e-10
    
    # Enable first context
    ureg.enable_contexts(c1)
    lb_with_c1 = one_kg.to("lb")
    assert abs(lb_with_c1.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-10  # 1 kg / 0.5 kg/lb = 2 lb
    
    # Enable second context - this should override the first!
    ureg.enable_contexts(c2)
    lb_with_c2 = one_kg.to("lb")
    assert abs(lb_with_c2.magnitude - 1.4285714285714286) < 1e-10  # 1 kg / 0.7 kg/lb = 1.4285714285714286 lb
    
    print("✅ Context redefinition overlay works correctly!")


def test_multiple_contexts_at_once():
    """Test enabling multiple contexts at once - last should win."""
    
    ureg = pint.UnitRegistry()
    c1 = pint.Context.from_lines(["@context c1", "meter = 100 cm"])  # Normal
    c2 = pint.Context.from_lines(["@context c2", "meter = 50 cm"])   # Half size
    c3 = pint.Context.from_lines(["@context c3", "meter = 200 cm"])  # Double size

    # Enable all three at once - c3 should win as it's last
    ureg.enable_contexts(c1, c2, c3)

    # Should be 1 meter = 200 cm (from c3, the last one)
    assert abs(result.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-10
    
    print("✅ Multiple contexts at once work correctly!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_context_redefinition_overlay_fix()
    test_multiple_contexts_at_once()
    print("🎉 All issue fix tests passed!")
